content: The Spencer Somers Foundation (SSF) is a charitable organization based in Minnesota. Its primary mission is to raise funds to support children with cancer and other underprivileged causes. The foundation was established in memory of Spencer J. Somers. Spencer J. Somers was born in Kansas City, Missouri, in 1972. In 1984, his family relocated to Edina, Minnesota. Known affectionately as Spense by his friends, he was an active participant in sports and well-liked at school. In June 1985, a lump was discovered in his abdomen, which was diagnosed as Primitive Neuroectodermal Tumor (PNET), a rare and aggressive form of cancer. The following month, Spencer underwent surgery to remove his spleen and part of his stomach, marking the first of many surgical procedures he would endure. Despite his diagnosis, Spencer remained active and engaged in life. Even as his physical condition deteriorated and he experienced hair loss, he continued to play basketball and baseball during his 9th and 10th grades. He also served as vice president of his junior class. Spencer was a talented writer and contributed to Edina High School's literary magazine, Images on the Wind. His work was recognized and he was invited to read his writings at the Loft bookstore in Minneapolis. In 1989, Spencer was crowned homecoming king at Edina High School, receiving a standing ovation from over 1,000 students at the homecoming rally. He also delivered one of the commencement speeches at his graduation ceremony in June, where he was again met with standing ovations. His classmates voted him most respected person. Despite his illness, Spencer walked the halls of his high school with a cheerful demeanor and an air of confidence. Spencer was deeply spiritual and a devout Christian. He served as vice president of the Cross View Lutheran Church Youth Group for two terms and was an active member of the Oasis Senior Youth Group. He volunteered with Sister Jean's Mercy Missions Cookie Cart, a bakery in North Minneapolis, and traveled to Kentucky to assist impoverished families in rebuilding their homes. His courage and resilience inspired the Edina community, and his battle with cancer garnered regional attention. In a 1989 interview with the Star Tribune, Spencer reflected on his personal struggles. Spencer briefly attended St. John’s University in Collegeville during his freshman year of college, but his illness forced him to return home after just one week. On November 9, 1990, Spencer Somers passed away at the age of 18. His death was widely mourned in the Twin Cities area, and his funeral was attended by many members of the community. In 1997, Spencer’s mother, Karen, and his favorite writing teacher, Carolyn Rebholz, posthumously published his journal entries and poetry in a tribute to his life titled Eating LIFE Cereal with a Bigger Spoon than Most. On November 9, 2000, exactly ten years after Spencer’s death, the Spencer Somers Foundation (SSF) was established. Its mission is to support underprivileged youth and individuals living with cancer. The foundation’s board of directors is chaired by Chris Davis, Spencer’s next-door neighbor and best friend. To further its goals, SSF created the Spencer Somers Fund, which provides financial assistance for expenses not covered by insurance and supports extracurricular activities for children with cancer and their families. One of the foundation’s initial projects involved raising funds for the Total Victory Christian Center, an outreach church in Minneapolis that supports a local congregation and at-risk inner-city youth. The Spencer Somers Foundation also served as the umbrella organization for the Phuket Project, which sent volunteers and aid to rebuild areas in southern Thailand devastated by the December 2004 tsunami. Over 700,000 baht and countless volunteer hours were dedicated to rebuilding homes, schools, businesses, temples, and community centers in Phang Nga Province, Khao Lak, and Phuket. To fund its activities, SSF organizes an annual Real McCoy Golf Challenge.
